tEn: The Future of Product Design with OpenAI's Head of Design
tZh: OpenAI 设计主管谈产品设计的未来
sEn: Ian Silber, Head of Product Design at OpenAI, discusses the evolving role of designers in the AI era, addressing industry uncertainty and the opportunities ahead.
sZh: OpenAI 设计主管 Ian Silber 探讨 AI 时代设计师角色的演变，回应行业不确定性并展望未来机遇。

consensus.en: Designers are currently the most unhappy in tech due to role uncertainty, but this is the best time to be a designer.
consensus.zh: 设计师目前是科技行业中最不快乐的群体，原因是角色不确定性，但现在是成为设计师的最佳时机。

consensus.en: AI is already an incredible product designer, but humans remain essential for understanding user needs and having a point of view.
consensus.zh: AI 已经是一位出色的产品设计师，但人类在理解用户需求和拥有观点方面仍然至关重要。

consensus.en: The design process is still messy and fluid; AI amplifies creativity but doesn't replace the iterative feedback loop.
consensus.zh: 设计过程仍然是混乱和流动的；AI 增强了创造力，但并未取代迭代反馈循环。

consensus.en: Designers should focus on outcomes, not processes, and embrace adaptability and exploration with AI tools.
consensus.zh: 设计师应关注结果而非过程，并拥抱对 AI 工具的适应性和探索。

consensus.en: The role of design is blurring with PM and engineering, but specialized roles remain valuable at scale.
consensus.zh: 设计的角色与产品管理和工程正在模糊，但在规模上，专业化角色仍然有价值。

consensus.en: AI tools like ChatGPT and Codex help designers prototype and think through ideas, enhancing their workflow.
consensus.zh: 像 ChatGPT 和 Codex 这样的 AI 工具帮助设计师进行原型设计和思考想法，增强了他们的工作流程。

contrarian.en: Designers are not behind; starting today gives you a leg up on most people due to the early stage of AI evolution.
contrarian.zh: 设计师并没有落后；由于 AI 发展的早期阶段，今天开始会让你领先于大多数人。

contrarian.en: The traditional design process of prototype, mock, test, research, iterate is no longer viable; speed is key.
contrarian.zh: 传统的设计流程（原型、模拟、测试、研究、迭代）已不再可行；速度是关键。

contrarian.en: AI is already a great product designer, contrary to the belief that it lacks design capabilities.
contrarian.zh: AI 已经是一位出色的产品设计师，这与认为它缺乏设计能力的观点相反。

contrarian.en: Engineers have 10-100x productivity gains, but designers haven't seen the same compression in their process.
contrarian.zh: 工程师的生产力提高了 10-100 倍，但设计师的流程并没有得到同样的压缩。

contrarian.en: The future of design roles may see more designers than engineers, reversing traditional ratios.
contrarian.zh: 未来设计角色的数量可能会超过工程师，扭转传统的比例。

contrarian.en: Embracing building in public and rapid iteration is more effective than obsessing over every detail.
contrarian.zh: 拥抱公开构建和快速迭代比纠结于每个细节更有效。

turns.en: Today my guest is Ian Silber, head of product design at OpenAI. Ian's been in this role for three years now, which is a lifetime in AI time. Prior to OpenAI, he was at Artifact, the news app from the founders of Instagram that I absolutely loved. Before that, he spent 8 years at Instagram. The role of design is in such an interesting place right now and Ian has such a unique and insightful and fascinating take on the future of product design and what the AI tools that we use everyday will look like in the future. A huge thank you to Cleo and Joel Loenstein for suggesting topics for this conversation. Before we get into it, don't forget to check out lennisproass.com for a year free of the hottest and most beautifully crafted AI products in the world available exclusively to Lenny's newsletter subscribers. With that, I bring you Ian Silber. Ian, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 今天我的嘉宾是 OpenAI 的产品设计主管 Ian Silber。Ian 担任这个职位已经三年了，在 AI 时代这算是很长的时间。在加入 OpenAI 之前，他在 Artifact 工作，那是 Instagram 创始人做的新闻应用，我个人非常喜欢。再之前，他在 Instagram 工作了 8 年。设计这个角色现在正处于一个非常有趣的阶段，Ian 对未来产品设计以及我们日常使用的 AI 工具会是什么样子，有着非常独特、深刻且迷人的见解。非常感谢 Cleo 和 Joel Loenstein 为这次对话提出话题建议。在我们开始之前，别忘了访问 lennisproass.com，可以免费获得一年全球最热门、设计最精美的 AI 产品，这些产品仅对 Lenny 的新闻通讯订阅者开放。接下来，有请 Ian Silber。Ian，非常感谢你来到这里。

turns.en: I'm so excited to be here. Thanks for having me.
turns.zh: 我非常高兴能来到这里。感谢你的邀请。

turns.en: I'm even more excited. Something that I'm very excited to get your take on. I don't know if you've watched me doing this, but I've been doing this sentiment survey of the tech workforce over the past couple years. I think it's the biggest survey of its kind where we basically survey people in tech about how they're feeling about their careers, their work, their roles, especially with the rise of AI this last year. And kind of surprisingly, designers and user researchers are just the most unhappy on every dimension, like every actual dimension. They're the most overwhelmed, the most anxious, the most the least optimistic, the most worried, the most tired, also the least likely to recommend their role to people entering the workforce. I'm curious if you're seeing this yourself in the design community, and if you are, what do you think is going on?
turns.zh: 我更加兴奋。有一件事我特别想听听你的看法。我不知道你是否看过我做的这个调查，过去几年我一直在做科技从业者的情绪调查。我认为这是同类调查中规模最大的，我们基本上调查科技从业者对他们的职业、工作、角色的感受，尤其是去年 AI 兴起之后。有点令人惊讶的是，设计师和用户研究员在每一个维度上都是最不开心的，真的是每一个维度。他们最感到不知所措、最焦虑、最不乐观、最担心、最疲惫，也最不愿意向进入职场的人推荐自己的角色。我很好奇你自己在设计社区是否也看到了这一点，如果是的话，你觉得是怎么回事？

turns.en: First of all, it's an incredible survey, and it's such great information to have as an industry. And I think it's something we need to unpack. And I see a mix for sure. I think I can speak most to design. I talk to a lot of designers that are very optimistic and very excited. And so in my world, luckily, I see a lot of that. But I can totally understand why people might be feeling very uncertain, right? Because there's so much discussion about, well, is the role changing? Should my expectations be different? And you know, well, do I need to do X, Y, and Z? Do I need to be shipping code every day? And someone who might be classically trained in a certain way of working now feeling like, "Oh my gosh, I need to really change everything." And I think it's to me right now it feels like the uncertainty of that I can totally understand, right? Because as an engineer, I think people have already sort of gone through that shift. We see that engineers are working totally different. And one thing I do hear, and this came up a lot in my own team when we did similar surveys internally, one of the big things that came up was that we see that engineers have 10 or sometimes like 100x their productivity, but our design team hasn't, right? Because the design process still takes time. It's still sometimes you have to try a bunch of things and throw them out, right? Versus maybe working with a coding agent, you ask it to do something, it's pretty binary now at this point, it usually sort of gets it pretty well. But the design process is really still very messy and fluid. You think you have a great idea and you try it and it sucks, and then you try it again and it sucks, and then you give it to users or internal, you get internal feedback and it's wrong, and you still have to go through that arduous and kind of messy but really fun process. And that hasn't really compressed in that you can get much more ideas out fast, but you still need that whole sort of feedback loop. There's the alignment of getting many people, especially in a bigger company like that, that still has a lot of overhead. So the point is that I think that we're unclear right now what is expected of a designer, and that lack of clarity I can see totally lead to some fears or some unease I guess. But on the other hand, I've seen that our designers, what's been great about OpenAI, is that we're such an experimental company. We are driven by research, and we treat our company as a research lab, and we totally embrace that. And that's a new thing that I really kind of learned and have come to love about OpenAI, is that it started as a research lab, that DNA is like deeply embedded in everything we do. And as designers, we look for people that don't have a background in AI but are really curious about the tools and how it can. And we found that just by supporting that excitement to explore, that people feel less pressure. It's not like you need to change the way you work, but it's more about encouraging exploration.
turns.zh: 首先，这是一项了不起的调查，作为行业来说，拥有这样的信息非常好。我认为我们需要深入探讨。我确实看到了各种情况。我想我最能代表设计领域发言。我和很多设计师聊过，他们非常乐观、非常兴奋。所以在我所处的环境中，幸运的是，我看到了很多这样的例子。但我完全能理解为什么人们可能会感到非常不确定，对吧？因为有太多讨论，比如：角色在改变吗？我的期望应该不同吗？还有，我需要做 X、Y、Z 吗？我需要每天发布代码吗？那些可能接受过传统工作方式训练的人，现在会觉得：“天哪，我真的需要彻底改变一切。”对我来说，现在这种不确定性，我完全能理解，对吧？因为作为工程师，我认为人们已经经历了那种转变。我们看到工程师的工作方式完全不同了。还有一件事我确实听到，而且这在我自己的团队中也经常出现，当我们做类似的内部调查时，出现的一个大问题是，我们看到工程师的生产力提高了 10 倍，有时甚至 100 倍，但我们的设计团队没有，对吧？因为设计过程仍然需要时间。有时候你仍然必须尝试很多东西，然后扔掉它们，对吧？相比之下，和编码智能体合作，你让它做某事，现在它相当二元化，通常能做得很好。但设计过程仍然非常混乱和流动。你以为你有一个好主意，你尝试了，结果很糟糕，然后你再试一次，还是很糟糕，然后你把它交给用户或内部人员，得到内部反馈，发现是错的，你仍然必须经历那个艰难、混乱但非常有趣的过程。这并没有真正压缩，你可以更快地产生更多想法，但你仍然需要那个完整的反馈循环。还需要协调很多人，尤其是在像这样的大公司里，这仍然有很多开销。所以重点是，我认为我们现在不清楚设计师的期望是什么，而这种缺乏清晰度，我完全可以看到会导致一些恐惧或不安。但另一方面，我看到了我们的设计师，OpenAI 的伟大之处在于，我们是一家非常实验性的公司。我们由研究驱动，我们把公司当作研究实验室，我们完全拥抱这一点。这是我真正学到并开始喜欢 OpenAI 的一点，它最初是一个研究实验室，这种 DNA 深深植根于我们所做的一切。作为设计师，我们寻找那些没有 AI 背景但对工具及其可能性非常好奇的人。我们发现，只要支持这种探索的热情，人们就会感到压力更小。这不是说你必须改变工作方式，而是鼓励探索。

turns.en: If you look at engineering, it's just a completely new job versus a few years ago. I'm curious how that translates to product design.
turns.zh: 如果你看看工程领域，和几年前相比，这完全是一份新工作。我很好奇这如何转化到产品设计上。

turns.en: Engineers have 10 or sometimes like 100x their productivity, but our design team hasn't because the design process still takes time. It's still sometimes you have to try a bunch of things and throw them out. Still very messy and fluid. We had a podcast with head of design Claude Code Jenny when she talked about there's been this traditional design process prototype mock test research iterate and now there's just no time for that.
turns.zh: 工程师的生产力提高了 10 倍，有时甚至 100 倍，但我们的设计团队没有，因为设计过程仍然需要时间。有时候你仍然必须尝试很多东西，然后扔掉它们。仍然非常混乱和流动。我们和 Claude Code 的设计主管 Jenny 做过一期播客，她谈到传统的设计流程是原型、模拟、测试、研究、迭代，而现在根本没有时间做这些。

turns.en: There's certain features for ChatGPT where we really obsess and we really spend a lot of time we try 100 things we throw out 99 we finally ship one and other things we really embrace building in public we take big swings and then we learn quickly. Do you think AI will ever be an extremely good product designer?
turns.zh: 对于 ChatGPT 的某些功能，我们真的非常执着，花了很多时间，我们尝试 100 个东西，扔掉 99 个，最后发布一个，而其他事情我们真的拥抱公开构建，我们大胆尝试，然后快速学习。你认为 AI 会成为一个极其出色的产品设计师吗？

turns.en: I think it already is an incredible product designer.
turns.zh: 我认为它已经是一个令人难以置信的产品设计师了。

turns.en: And when we've done that, when I go and talk to both very senior designers and early career designers at our company, they're so excited because—I was literally just asking some people before this because I wanted to get some different takes—and they, you know, I think the feeling is that they have so much more ability to be creative, to express themselves, to try bad ideas and throw them out. You can just really move through lots of different ideas, and it becomes this incredible way to create. And the things that I'm seeing from my team, the bar is raising. The thinking is getting stronger the more that they're using these tools. So, I think for the people that are starting to embrace this, they're starting to feel really excited and realizing that they have so much agency as designers, and so much more ability to have really high impact as a designer.
turns.zh: 当我们做到这一点后，我去和我们公司里非常资深的设计师以及刚起步的设计师交流，他们都特别兴奋——因为我在这次对话之前真的问了一些人，想听听不同的看法——他们，你知道，我觉得他们的感受是，他们有了更多的创造力，能更好地表达自己，能尝试糟糕的想法然后抛弃它们。你可以快速尝试很多不同的想法，这成了一种不可思议的创作方式。而且我从团队身上看到的是，标准在提高。他们越用这些工具，思考就越深入。所以，我觉得对于那些开始拥抱这一切的人来说，他们开始感到非常兴奋，意识到作为设计师，他们有了更多的自主权，也有了更大的能力去产生真正高的影响力。

turns.en: What I'd love to do in this conversation is help folks that are in that bucket of 'well, this sucks and things aren't going well,' because as you said, and this is exactly what we found in that survey, about half of people are having the best time of their career, having the most fun, the most optimistic about where things are going, and then the other half are not having a really hard time. And exactly what you said, the people that are having a great time report—the strongest correlation—is they feel amplified by AI. It's actually making them better. And that's the way you described engineers; they're seeing that now. They're like, 'Holy, I can do so much more.' And so just to kind of reinforce the point you're making, think attributes of people that are doing well: feel amplified, very curious, have time to explore, feel like they can be more creative. Is there any more thing more along those lines, just patterns of people that are doing really well and having a great time, that might be helpful for people to hear that are not having a good time?
turns.zh: 在这次对话中，我想做的是帮助那些处于“这太糟糕了，事情进展不顺利”状态的人，因为正如你所说，这正是我们在调查中发现的：大约一半的人正处于职业生涯中最美好的时光，玩得最开心，对未来最乐观，而另一半人则过得很艰难。而且正如你所说，那些过得很开心的人报告的最强相关性是，他们感到被 AI 放大。AI 确实让他们变得更好。这就是你描述工程师的方式；他们现在看到了这一点。他们会说：“天哪，我能做这么多。”所以，为了强化你的观点，想想那些表现良好的人的特点：感到被放大、非常好奇、有时间探索、觉得自己更有创造力。还有没有更多类似的模式，关于那些表现良好、过得很开心的人，可能对现在不开心的人有帮助？

turns.en: What I see in the folks that I think are really embracing this, right, they are using it every step of the process to help them, right? And I think it helps—we have a community, of course, of designers that are all trying this together. So if there's any way to kind of find that, and that's something that we should think about more as a broader community, how we kind of help each other. But I think that learning different ways of working, right, and so it might be okay: 'I have this idea, let me just actually start by trying what if I just threw this right into Codex or Claude or whatever tool you use, like throw it into an agent to help you think about it, to help you prototype it, just try a different way of working.' It doesn't necessarily mean that that has to be the exact right way. But I don't know. I think we found that people that are embracing this, that are adaptable—I think adaptability is another term that we all hear a lot now, but it's so true. It's like knowing that this stuff changes very quickly. What didn't work yesterday might work today. I mean, literally within six months, this entire industry has shifted. I remember I was actually out on paternity leave towards the end of last year, and I was working on some side projects. I was trying some coding agents, and it just worked, but it just kept running into these hiccups. And then like a month later, Codex drops, and I try it again, and it's like, 'Oh my gosh, it just works.' And that I think changes a lot of the design process, because now all of a sudden, if you do have an idea, you can like plop it in there and just try it. And so anyways, I think it's just really about not being scared. I think another thing to think about is that we're so early. We're like so in early innings of this entire evolution, right? It feels like things have changed a lot, and it feels like maybe we're pretty far into this shift. But the good news for anybody who is trying to design or get into design, whether again like if you're early career or late career, or you never even actually designed anything but you've been thinking about it, is that we're all figuring this out as we go. Nobody has some perfect answer about how the design process should work. And it's whatever you think is working today will probably change again. And so I think what's encouraging about this is that nobody should feel like behind right now. I think that if you literally started today, you're going to have a leg up on pretty much most people. And just really thinking about how you can just make great stuff. And there's just so much opportunity to change the way you work or to just make great things. And what we think is really cutting-edge today will look so archaic in a year, let alone a month. And that's something I've learned—I've been at OpenAI for three years, and I think about the stuff that we were working on when I first joined. I mean, I remember getting a demo of our early voice mode that we hadn't shipped, or computer use that barely worked. And now it's become—it literally has become part of the process of how we design. We use both of those tools to build software. And so anyways, the point is it's changing very quickly. We're all extremely early in this process, and nobody really has it figured out.
turns.zh: 我在那些真正拥抱这一切的人身上看到的是，他们在流程的每一步都用它来帮助自己，对吧？而且我认为这有帮助——我们当然有一个设计师社区，大家都在共同尝试。所以如果有办法找到那种方式，这是我们作为更广泛的社区应该更多思考的，我们如何互相帮助。但我认为学习不同的工作方式，对吧，所以可能可以这样：“我有个想法，让我先试试，如果我把这个直接扔进 Codex 或 Claude 或你用的任何工具，比如扔给一个智能体来帮你思考，帮你做原型，就试试不同的工作方式。”这不一定非得是正确的方式。但我不知道。我觉得我们发现那些拥抱这一切、适应性强的人——我认为适应性是我们现在经常听到的另一个词，但它非常真实。就像知道这些东西变化很快。昨天不奏效的今天可能就奏效了。我的意思是，在六个月内，整个行业都变了。我记得去年年底我休陪产假，当时在做一些副业项目。我尝试了一些编码智能体，它确实能工作，但总是遇到一些小问题。然后大约一个月后，Codex 发布了，我再试一次，就像“天哪，它就这么工作了。”我认为这改变了很多设计流程，因为现在如果你有个想法，你可以直接把它放进去试试。所以无论如何，我认为关键就是不要害怕。我觉得另一件要考虑的事情是，我们还非常早。我们正处于整个演进的早期阶段，对吧？感觉事情已经变了很多，也许我们已经走得很远了。但对任何想设计或进入设计领域的人来说，无论你是早期职业还是晚期职业，或者你从未真正设计过任何东西但一直在考虑，好消息是我们都在摸索中前进。没有人对设计流程应该如何运作有完美的答案。而且你认为今天有效的东西，可能明天又会变。所以我认为令人鼓舞的是，现在没有人应该觉得自己落后了。我认为如果你今天才开始，你会比大多数人更有优势。而且只要真正思考如何做出伟大的东西。有太多机会去改变你的工作方式，或者只是做出伟大的东西。我们今天认为最前沿的东西，一年后就会显得非常过时，更不用说一个月了。这是我学到的——我在 OpenAI 工作了三年，我想起我刚加入时我们正在做的事情。我记得我们早期语音模式的演示，还没发布，或者几乎不能用的计算机使用功能。现在它已经成了我们设计流程的一部分。我们用这两个工具来构建软件。所以无论如何，重点是变化非常快。我们都处于这个过程的极早期，没有人真正搞明白了。

transcript.sec: Best time to be a designer

turns.en: I love that you've also, when we were chatting ahead of this year, you actually told me you believe this is the best time in history to be a designer.
turns.zh: 我很喜欢你之前也说过，在我们今年聊天的时候，你告诉我你相信这是历史上成为设计师的最佳时机。

turns.en: Yeah, I mean, I truly believe this. I can't even imagine... So, history lesson: when I was getting into design, I was in my teenage years. To learn things, I was learning design and code, and you could view source on an HTML web page and see how things were built. That was how you had to learn. There were tools like Dreamweaver that were actually really cool. But to compare those to today, if I were just getting into design, the fact that you can learn so quickly and go from an idea to a working version in minutes—it's just so expressive. I think anybody can be a designer. And as more software and products are made, the human element of design is going to become more and more important. It's always been the case that companies with great design can stand out, but I think it's going to be even more important. Products that fully understand their users and make something delightful, when anybody can make anything, that's going to become one of the most important dimensions of a product, and that's how people will evaluate it. So designers stand at that core job. On top of that, designers are much more empowered. I was talking to some friends thinking about starting a company, and we discussed the ratio of design to engineering. At a startup, it might have been one designer to fifteen engineers. But they were talking about maybe two designers and one engineer—one really good engineer to make sure the engineering is rock solid, but two really creative people to think about how to build the product. So there's a huge opportunity for designers. Internally, we see that more and more: designers are completely empowered to take an idea or an early research concept and figure out how to package it into something people want to use, solving an unmet need. That's a designer's job. So maybe more people will start to think of themselves as designers. Either way, I truly think it's the best time to be a designer.
turns.zh: 是的，我真心相信这一点。我甚至无法想象……来点历史课：当我开始接触设计时，我还在青少年时期。要学习东西，我学着设计和编程，你可以查看 HTML 网页的源代码，看看东西是怎么构建的。那就是你必须学习的方式。当时有像 Dreamweaver 这样的工具，其实很酷。但和今天相比，如果我现在才开始做设计，你能学得这么快，几分钟内就能从想法变成可用的版本——这太有表现力了。我认为任何人都可以成为设计师。随着越来越多的软件和产品被制造出来，设计中的人性元素会变得越来越重要。一直以来，拥有优秀设计的公司都能脱颖而出，但我觉得这会变得更加重要。当任何人都能做出任何东西时，那些真正理解用户并创造出令人愉悦体验的产品，将成为产品最重要的维度之一，人们也会以此评价产品。所以设计师就站在这个核心岗位上。除此之外，设计师被赋予了更多权力。我和一些朋友聊天，他们想创业，我们讨论了设计与工程的比例。在初创公司，可能是一个设计师对十五个工程师。但他们说也许会有两个设计师和一个工程师——一个真正优秀的工程师来确保工程稳固，但两个真正有创造力的人来思考如何构建产品。所以设计师有巨大的机会。在内部，我们越来越多地看到：设计师完全有能力把一个想法或早期研究概念，包装成人们想用的东西，解决客户未满足的需求。这就是设计师的工作。所以也许会有更多人开始把自己视为设计师。不管怎样，我真心认为这是成为设计师的最佳时机。

turns.en: So along those lines, when Mark Andre was on the podcast, he had this hilarious way of describing the state of the product world right now. He's like, basically there's this three-way standoff. PMs, engineers, designers—they all think the other roles are going to go away and they're the ones that are going to win in the end. It's like the Spider-Man meme where they're all pointing at each other. I'm curious because I can see a case for each role becoming the dominant role. And I completely agree with you that with all the tools being shipped, there's like a thousand-fold explosion in products being shipped, endless streams of things to pay attention to. You'd think design would be such an opportunity to differentiate and stand out. I haven't seen that yet in an acceleration of design hires and an explosion as you said, like two designers to one engineer. Do you think that's coming? Why do you think that hasn't happened yet? Do you think it's as you said, just early, and people will realize, oh wow, we need a lot more designers? What do you think is going on?
turns.zh: 顺着这个思路，当马克·安德森上播客时，他用一种搞笑的方式描述了当前产品世界的状态。他说，基本上有三方对峙。产品经理、工程师、设计师——他们都认为其他角色会消失，而自己最终会胜出。就像蜘蛛侠表情包那样，互相指着对方。我很好奇，因为我能看到每个角色成为主导角色的理由。我完全同意你的看法，随着所有工具被推出，产品数量呈千倍爆炸式增长，有源源不断的东西需要关注。你会觉得设计应该是差异化并脱颖而出的机会。但我还没看到设计招聘的加速，也没看到你说的那种爆炸，比如两个设计师对一个工程师。你觉得这会到来吗？为什么你认为这还没发生？你觉得是不是像你说的，还为时过早，人们会意识到“哇，我们需要更多设计师”？你觉得现在是什么情况？

turns.en: We might start to see that happen more. Or if anything, we might start to see engineers wanting to become a little bit more design-focused. I also think that designers are getting more productive. It's not necessarily the same direct output of engineers 10xing, but we are seeing that designers are able to do a lot more. But no, I mean, I think that that is something we're always thinking about and evolving. The other thing I wanted to talk about is the difference between PM, engineering, and design—are they all blurring together? My point of view is that they definitely are, and there's always been overlap as far as I've seen it. I've seen designers that are like really good product manager type archetypes but can design, and I've seen designers that are like really good polish engineer types. So I've always found that these single-siloed role definitions don't really make sense. It's just that at big companies you have to have a ladder to put people on so you can organize. But in reality, when you look at a team, you see people with various strengths and different roles. So I've always seen that. The lines have always been blurry, but they're becoming blurrier for sure. But the other thing is, I do still think—and maybe this is from a slightly larger company perspective—you still need people with certain responsibilities. Because if you have one person expected to design, rally a team, align a whole company, do all the work a PM does, and also be designing and engineering, it might be hard to find one person good at all those skills. So I still find a lot of value, for example, in having an excellent PM who can help rally multiple teams, sharpen the perspective or problem space a team focuses on, and help with resourcing. So I do think there will still be value in people focusing on different parts of building a project or product.
turns.zh: 我们可能会开始看到这种情况更多发生。或者，我们可能会看到工程师想变得更注重设计。我也认为设计师的生产力在提高。这不一定是像工程师那样直接 10 倍输出，但我们确实看到设计师能做的事情更多了。但我的意思是，这是我们一直在思考和演变的事情。我还想谈谈产品经理、工程和设计之间的区别——它们是不是都在融合？我的观点是，它们确实在融合，而且据我所见，一直都有重叠。我见过一些设计师，他们很像优秀的产品经理类型，但也能做设计；我也见过一些设计师，他们很像优秀的打磨型工程师。所以我一直觉得，这些孤立的单一角色定义其实没有意义。只是在大公司，你得有晋升阶梯来安排人，以便组织。但实际上，当你观察一个团队时，你会看到有不同优势和不同角色的人。所以我一直这么看。这些界限一直很模糊，但肯定越来越模糊了。但另一方面，我仍然认为——也许这是从稍大公司的角度来看——你仍然需要有特定职责的人。因为如果一个人被期望做设计、团结团队、协调整个公司、做产品经理的所有工作，同时还要设计和工程，那可能很难找到一个擅长所有这些技能的人。所以，例如，我仍然觉得有一个优秀的产品经理很有价值，他能帮助团结多个团队，锐化团队关注的观点或问题空间，并帮助解决资源问题。所以我确实认为，专注于项目或产品不同部分的人仍然会有价值。

transcript.sec: Roles and Responsibilities in AI Era

turns.en: That doesn't mean there isn't more fluidity between roles, but having someone generally responsible for these things, or an engineer who ensures the output is sound and leads to something that works for the broader system, is still important.
turns.zh: 这并不意味着角色之间没有更多的流动性，但有一个总体负责这些事情的人，或者一个确保输出完全可靠并最终能服务于整个系统的工程师，仍然很重要。

turns.en: I completely agree. So just to make sure I understand what you're saying: there's talk about all the roles blurring, like maybe we'll all just be builders and do everything. You're saying that's not going to happen. I'm picturing Venn diagrams of product, design, engineering converging, but you're saying they'll continue to stay their own roles—there'll be a PM, a designer, an engineer—but each can do more of the other roles.
turns.zh: 我完全同意。所以确认一下我理解得对不对：大家都在说角色会模糊，也许我们都会成为建造者，什么都做。而你说这不会发生。我想象的是产品、设计、工程的维恩图在交汇，但你说它们会保持各自的角色——会有产品经理、设计师、工程师——但每个人都能更多地承担其他角色。

turns.en: I think that's right. And again, this isn't a blanket statement, because if you're at a startup, it's very different. If I were starting a company right now, I'd hire the best generalists I could think of—people who can fluidly move between roles. But maybe that's always been true. At a bigger company, though, I've seen designers who are incredible at designing but could really use a product manager to help hone their thinking and the operations of it all. The point is, taking the people out of it, there are different hats you need to wear to build great software, and those continue to be important functions.
turns.zh: 我想这是对的。再说一次，这不是一概而论，因为如果你在创业公司，情况就非常不同。如果我现在要创办一家公司，我会雇佣我能想到的最优秀的通才——那些能在不同角色间灵活切换的人。但也许这一直都是如此。不过，在大公司里，我见过一些设计师，他们设计能力很强，但确实需要产品经理来帮助他们打磨思维以及整个工作流程。关键是，抛开具体的人，要构建优秀的软件需要扮演不同的角色，而这些角色仍然是重要的职能。

turns.en: This begs the question: do you think AI will ever be an extremely good product designer? It's interesting to ask you this because on one hand, you're like, 'Oh yeah, ChatGPT is going to become incredible at everything.' On the other hand, it's hard for a head of design to say, 'Oh no, design will be done by AI.' I'm curious to get your take. It sounds crazy, but engineers never thought it would be able to write code the way it does now. So, thoughts on just how good AI will get?
turns.zh: 这就引出了一个问题：你认为 AI 会成为一个极其出色的产品设计师吗？问你这个问题很有意思，因为一方面，你会说“哦，是的，ChatGPT 会在所有事情上变得不可思议”。另一方面，设计主管很难说“哦，不，设计会被 AI 完成”。我很好奇你的看法。这听起来很疯狂，但工程师们从未想过 AI 能像现在这样写代码。所以，你对 AI 能达到多高水平有什么想法？

turns.en: Maybe one way to put it is: I think it already is an incredible product designer. It really is already great. The cool thing is it's accessible to every single person—it's a tool anyone can use. Now, that doesn't mean it's the best visual designer, or best at information hierarchy, typography, or even user experience and interaction design. It's not necessarily the best at any of those. It's impossible to predict where things are going. As I said earlier, how much has changed in three years? Of course they'll continue to get better. But the way we think about it—and I really believe this—is we're building tools to enable people to be more creative, to do more, to build more. So it's already a great designer, but it's at your fingertips to figure out how to use it and get the best out of it.
turns.zh: 也许可以这样说：我认为它已经是一个不可思议的产品设计师了。它确实已经很出色了。酷的是它对每个人都是可用的——它是任何人都能使用的工具。但这并不意味着它是最好的视觉设计师，或者最擅长信息层级、排版，甚至用户体验和交互设计。它不一定在这些方面是最强的。我们无法预测事情会如何发展。正如我之前所说，三年内变化有多大？当然它们会继续变得更好。但我们的思考方式——我真心相信这一点——是我们正在构建工具，让人们更有创造力，做得更多，构建更多。所以它已经是一个伟大的设计师了，但如何利用它并发挥其最大价值，就掌握在你手中。

turns.en: Where do you think human brains will continue to be most valuable as AI gets better at product design specifically? What are the remaining areas for us to be useful?
turns.zh: 随着 AI 在产品设计方面变得更好，你认为人脑在哪些方面仍然最有价值？我们还有哪些领域可以发挥作用？

turns.en: Truly understanding what people need. The human feedback loop of watching people use something and understanding that. Inventing something new. And then of course there's the pure human take—like, 'Oh, somebody made this, somebody had a point of view about this.' I think that will stand out more and more. It's important for a designer to really hone: what is my point of view? Who am I building this for and why? As AI becomes better and better, there will always be an opportunity to stand out and push—how can you push that even further?
turns.zh: 真正理解人们的需求。观察人们使用某物并理解其中的人性反馈循环。发明新事物。然后当然还有纯粹的人类视角——比如“哦，有人做了这个，有人对此有自己的观点”。我认为这会越来越突出。对设计师来说，真正磨练自己的观点很重要：我的观点是什么？我为谁而建，为什么？随着 AI 变得越来越好，总会有机会脱颖而出并推动——你如何能进一步推动这一点？

turns.en: Yeah, that touches on a conversation I had with the PM of Codex. I asked him just why is AI not good at design? It's actually gotten better since that conversation, which was just a month or two ago. He had a number of reasons. One is that part of great product design is doing something new. So if it's trained on all the most interesting websites today, it's like, 'Okay, but that's not interesting anymore.' The other point he made is that AI researchers aren't innately great at design, so they may not understand exactly what it takes to train a model to be really good at this. Thoughts? What do you think it'll take to get AI to be much, much better at product design?
turns.zh: 是的，这让我想起我和 Codex 的产品经理的一次对话。我问他为什么 AI 不擅长设计？实际上，自从那次对话以来（也就一两个月前），它已经变得更好了。他给出了几个原因。一个是，优秀的产品设计的一部分是做一些新的事情。所以如果它是在今天所有最有趣的网站上训练的，那就像“好吧，但那已经不再有趣了”。他提出的另一点是，AI 研究人员本身并不天生擅长设计，所以他们可能不完全理解训练一个模型真正擅长设计需要什么。你怎么看？你认为要让 AI 在产品设计上变得更好，需要什么？

turns.en: The new thing is interesting, right? Because everything we're doing is trying to design something that hasn't existed before. If you look at great products from the last 10 or 20 years, take the iPhone—we were designing for multi-touch, and that opened up a whole new interaction paradigm. There's no training data for that. You have to really try to understand this new thing. Then you had Instagram, which embraced the fact that everybody had mobile phones. And Snapchat is another good example of great design—it was a strange interaction design, but it completely flipped on its head the way people might want to communicate. To me, that's great design: truly understanding that people have this problem or unmet need, and building it in a unique way. So yes, there's that fresh new way. And now with AI, we're designing how do you talk to AI with your voice, or how do you use an agent to carry out tasks for you? There isn't a lot of precedent. So I think humans are able to do a really good job evaluating what good is, or at least trying a bunch of things and learning along the way with people.
turns.zh: 新事物很有趣，对吧？因为我们所做的一切都是在尝试设计以前不存在的东西。看看过去 10 年或 20 年里的伟大产品，比如 iPhone——我们当时在为多点触控设计，这开启了一个全新的交互范式。没有针对它的训练数据。你必须真正去理解这个新事物。然后是 Instagram，它拥抱了每个人都拥有手机这一事实。Snapchat 是另一个伟大设计的好例子——它是一种奇怪的交互相式设计，但它完全颠覆了人们可能想要交流的方式。对我来说，这就是伟大的设计：真正理解人们有这个问题或未满足的需求，并以独特的方式构建它。所以是的，有那种全新的方式。而现在有了 AI，我们正在设计如何用语音与 AI 对话，或者如何使用智能体为你执行任务？没有太多先例。所以我认为人类能够很好地评估什么是好的，或者至少尝试很多事情，并在这个过程中与人一起学习。

transcript.sec: Human in the loop and hiring trends

turns.en: And so um I don't know, but again, like all this stuff changes really quickly. It's hard to say, but uh I think um I think there's a lot of reasons why uh having that human in the loop is going to be so important. And kind of following that thread of the human in the loop when you're hiring designers these days, what's kind of trending up in what you look for, what you think is more and more important in the designers that will be successful today, especially at OpenAI, what's trending down with anything?
turns.zh: 所以，嗯，我不知道，但同样，所有这些东西变化都很快，很难说，但我觉得，嗯，我认为有很多原因使得人类参与其中变得如此重要。顺着这个思路，当你现在招聘设计师时，什么趋势在上升？你在寻找什么？你认为如今成功的设计师，尤其是在 OpenAI，哪些特质越来越重要？有什么在下降吗？

turns.en: This might be a luxury of having a slightly larger team, but if you're, you know, at our scale, um, you know, but even at at a startup or a smaller company, I think this still be true. I really believe in hiring a well-rounded team that has many different strengths. So, I think it's important to have kind of like your handful of or or the right ratio of sort of generalists that can kind of do everything, but uh you know, we also hire like incredible visual designers or we have like like a really amazing sort of brand team that helps us with kind of like the sort of maybe Yeah. expression of our brand both out and in a in the product um or great prototypers or um you know um and so I think that rounding that out or or great sort of product thinkers that are a little bit more strategic or people that are like really obsess over like the very cutting edge of where these things are going and I haven't found that one designer necessarily checks every single one of those boxes. I think people just naturally are, you know, drawn to certain things and I think embracing that when you build a team is actually like um if you if you have the luxury of doing that is like really valuable. Okay. So that's like my a broad statement. But then as far as what we look for, we do definitely, you know, I always tell candidates, we do not expect you to have a background in AI because again, this is evolving so quickly, but we definitely expect high curiosity about it and and and a high aptitude to jumping in and learning how how you know how you're going to use this in your process, how it works. and not just how you use it in your process, but how especially for us like how you're going to create tools to enable more people to use it. turns.zh: 凯文·威尔，你的前首席产品官，在播客上说过一句话让我印象深刻。正如你所说，人们总是批评“它只是一个聊天框。为什么它从未改变？”尽管它已经改变了，但它仍然是一个聊天机器人。他提出了一个很好的观点：什么界面能很好地跨越广泛的智能频谱？实际上就是对话。想想人类，我们与低智商到高智商的人交谈。我们都可以互相交谈，这实际上是包装越来越智能的东西的一个非常好的界面。

turns.en: Yeah. And I think we're seeing what's been a really fun design space for us. There are two things we think about. One is how we can help you express your intent better, right? We don't want you to have to think about being a perfect prompt engineer, but how do we teach you that 'oh, this is something the model can help me with,' and then how do we make sure we best understand what you want? So we recently shipped some features where if you ask an open-ended question, it can follow up with some follow-up questions that you can tap through and answer, versus having to type everything out. Another good example is, once you actually ask it to do something, the chat transcript doesn't need to be purely text. We've seen these evolve so far from what it was when ChatGPT just launched. It's no longer just a pure chatbot; it has many features within that. A good example is what we call writing blocks. You ask it to write you a letter or an email, and it now contains that email in a block that you can directly manipulate. You can type with it, brainstorm, edit little bits and parts, copy just that, and that has made the interaction much better. We're seeing the same thing with image generation and creating special tools for that kind of mode. I think that's where the UI is going to continue to evolve: how do we make it so if you're a designer, maybe ChatGPT should look different or have different affordances? Or if you're a data scientist, or you're using this to run your home or your personal life, maybe it should work or look differently. So understanding the context and giving you different affordances based on that is something we're thinking a lot about.
turns.zh: 是的。我认为我们正在看到对我们来说一个非常有趣的设计空间。我们考虑两件事。一是如何帮助你更好地表达你的意图，对吧？我们不希望你必须考虑成为一个完美的提示工程师，但我们如何教你“哦，这是模型可以帮助我的事情”，然后我们如何确保我们最好地理解你想要什么？所以我们最近推出了一些功能，如果你问一个开放式问题，它可以提出一些后续问题，你可以点击回答，而不必全部输入。另一个好例子是，一旦你实际要求它做某事，聊天记录不必纯粹是文本。我们已经看到这些从 ChatGPT 刚推出时演变了很多。它不再只是一个纯粹的聊天机器人；它内部有许多功能。一个很好的例子是我们所谓的“写作块”。你让它给你写一封信或一封电子邮件，它现在把邮件放在一个你可以直接操作的块中。你可以与它一起输入、头脑风暴、编辑小部分、只复制那部分，这使交互变得更好。我们在图像生成和为那种模式创建特殊工具方面也看到了同样的情况。我认为这就是 UI 将继续演变的地方：我们如何做到，如果你是一名设计师，也许 ChatGPT 应该看起来不同或具有不同的功能？或者如果你是一名数据科学家，或者你用它来管理你的家庭或个人生活，也许它应该以不同的方式工作或看起来不同。所以理解上下文并根据上下文给你不同的功能是我们正在思考很多的事情。

turns.en: In terms of the vision and future of where all this goes, I know this is always evolving, but is there a sense of what the future of ChatGPT and Codex is? I know there's this idea of a super app. You talked about voice, this personal assistant idea. What's a way you think about where this goes long term?
turns.zh: 关于这一切走向的愿景和未来，我知道这总是在演变，但有没有一种对 ChatGPT 和 Codex 未来的感觉？我知道有超级应用的想法。你谈到了语音，这个个人助理的想法。你如何看待长期的发展方向？

turns.en: I think it will start to become more and more adaptive to all the context of your life. I think proactivity is a big untapped part of the experience that we're really excited to think about. We're starting to see this with ChatGPT work now, where it actually has pretty good suggestions based on your calendar or your Slack or these different inputs and external context. I think that's going to become more and more important and shift the way you use it. I think voice, as we just had a step change in the model that feels much more natural, and I can only imagine how that's going to feel in two or three years as it gets better and better. I do love interacting with ChatGPT, especially voice, when I just want to quickly say something. And I think its ability to go not just from asking questions but actually doing things for you is key.
turns.zh: 我认为它将开始变得越来越适应你生活的所有背景。我认为主动性是体验中一个巨大的未开发部分，我们非常兴奋去思考。我们现在开始在 ChatGPT 工作中看到这一点，它实际上根据你的日历、Slack 或这些不同的输入和外部背景提供了相当好的建议。我认为这将变得越来越重要，并改变你使用它的方式。我认为语音，正如我们刚刚在模型上经历了一个阶跃变化，感觉更加自然，我只能想象在两三年后它会感觉如何，随着它变得越来越好。我确实喜欢与 ChatGPT 互动，尤其是语音，当我想快速说点什么的时候。而且我认为它的能力不仅是从提问，而是实际为你做事，这是关键。

turns.en: Um, that's all going to change, and hopefully all of this gets simpler as we do it too. You know, when we think of the super app, I think eventually we really think of the idea, especially for our broad consumer base, that there should be this one universal input that you can ask, that knows when it needs to answer really quickly, or whether it should be chatty, or whether it should go off and do work for you. And so that's a big excitement that we can get to: how can we continue to simplify the experience such that you shouldn't have to think about how this works? You shouldn't have to think about what model you're on or what sort of speed you're using. That goes back to balancing the different personas and user needs. Of course, we want to expose that for the right people, but then we want to make sure that we can get a default experience that works great for most people.
turns.zh: 嗯，这一切都会改变，而且随着我们推进，希望一切也会变得更简单。你知道，当我们想到超级应用时，最终我们真正想的是，尤其是对于我们的广大消费者群体，应该有一个通用的输入入口，你可以向它提问，它知道什么时候需要快速回答，什么时候应该闲聊，或者是否应该去为你执行任务。所以，我们的一大兴奋点就是：如何继续简化体验，让你不必去想它是怎么运作的。你不必去想你在用什么模型，或者你用的是哪种速度。这又回到了平衡不同用户角色和需求的问题。当然，我们想为合适的人提供这些选项，但我们也想确保能提供一个对大多数人都很好用的默认体验。

turns.en: But yeah, I think it's going to be really proactive. I do think that we're going to get much richer input through voice and richer visual outputs that are more interactive. I think that you'll start to build more durable workflows with attributes that you can use over and over. Right now, a lot of times it feels like you're coming and starting from scratch each time. And we want to really make this the tool that you can use to help you with whatever task you have.
turns.zh: 但没错，我认为它会变得非常主动。我确实认为我们将通过语音获得更丰富的输入，以及更丰富、更具交互性的视觉输出。我认为你会开始构建更持久的工作流程，这些流程带有你可以反复使用的属性。现在，很多时候感觉你每次都要从头开始。我们真的想让它成为你可以用来处理任何任务的工具。

turns.en: This all sounds wonderful. I can't wait.
turns.zh: 这一切听起来太棒了，我等不及了。

transcript.sec: Advice for Ian at day one

turns.en: Uh, just kind of zooming out a little bit, and then I want to talk a little bit to designers again, but you're in this epic role right now. I imagine there's a lot of surprises as you entered OpenAI and took on this role. What's something you wish you'd known? What's something you wish you could whisper into Ian of day one to give you some advice?
turns.zh: 嗯，稍微拉远一点，然后我想再和设计师们聊聊，但你现在担任这个重要的角色。我想你进入 OpenAI 并承担这个角色时，一定有很多惊喜。有什么你希望自己当时就知道的事情？有什么你希望能对第一天的 Ian 耳语，给他一些建议？

turns.en: I mean, so many things. I think the first one is recognizing that we're really early. And instead, I was actually pretty intimidated coming to OpenAI, if I'm being honest. I remember, okay, interviewing. Oh no, I got to, you know, GPT-4 had kind of recently come out, and what GPT, like I was like, what is all this stuff? I was using it, and I was using the stuff, but I didn't feel like I had a true understanding of it. And to be honest, I still have so much to learn. So that idea of 'you are early, we're figuring this out' is what I would want to hear.
turns.zh: 我是说，太多了。我想第一点是认识到我们真的很早。说实话，我当初来 OpenAI 时其实挺忐忑的。我记得，好吧，面试的时候。哦不，我得，你知道，GPT-4 刚出来不久，还有 GPT，我当时想，这都是些什么？我在用，我也在用这些东西，但我并没有真正理解它。说实话，我还有很多要学的。所以，那种“你来得早，我们还在摸索”的想法，是我当时想听到的。

turns.en: And the other thing that I found, and for me this is more of a personal thing, it's less about AI or anything, but I stepped into a really different role. Most of my career I've managed, I definitely managed before, but never at a scale that's growing so fast, and at a company that is so different. The role was just every day was something new. And for a long time I felt like I'm kind of bad at this, or I don't know what I'm doing. And then I went and talked to friends that had led really large design teams, or were in a similar transition as me, and they all felt exactly the same, or the problems that I had were not unique.
turns.zh: 另一件我发现的事情，对我来说这更个人化，不太关乎 AI 或其他，而是我进入了一个非常不同的角色。我职业生涯大部分时间都在管理，我之前确实管理过，但从未在增长如此之快的规模上，而且是在一家如此不同的公司。这个角色每天都是新的。很长一段时间，我觉得自己有点不擅长这个，或者我不知道自己在做什么。然后我去和那些领导过大型设计团队的朋友，或者和我有类似转型经历的朋友聊了聊，他们都有完全一样的感觉，或者我的问题并不独特。

turns.en: And so, this is more personal advice, but I think at any stage of your career there's that feeling of impostor syndrome, like 'what am I doing? I don't know how to do this.' Finding people you can talk to who are going through similar things, you'll find that there's usually a lot of shared challenges and struggles. And having that, whether it's a mentor or just a buddy that is impartial and out of it, has been really helpful to me. Finding that community has been helpful. So, that, and then understanding that this is all so new and evolving really quickly.
turns.zh: 所以，这是更个人化的建议，但我认为在职业生涯的任何阶段，都会有那种冒充者综合症的感觉，比如“我在做什么？我不知道该怎么做。”找到可以交谈的、正在经历类似事情的人，你会发现通常有很多共同的挑战和挣扎。拥有那样的人，无论是导师还是只是一个中立的、置身事外的伙伴，对我帮助很大。找到那个社群很有帮助。所以，就是这样，然后理解这一切都是如此新颖，并且发展得非常快。

turns.en: That is extremely helpful to hear. Elena Vera had this really great post. I don't know if you know her. She's at How to Grow to Lovable right now. She had this great post called 'Stop the AI confidence theater' where she just kind of talks about how all these people just keep posting all these things they've done with AI and all the ways it's changed their life, and they're killing it, figured it all out. And really, it's like very few of these things are actually that great and working. And it's just like, stop pretending like you've figured it all out.
turns.zh: 听到这些非常有帮助。Elena Vera 发了一篇很棒的文章。我不知道你是否认识她。她现在在 How to Grow to Lovable。她发了一篇很棒的文章，叫《停止 AI 自信剧场》，她在文中谈到，所有这些人都不断发布他们用 AI 做的事情，以及 AI 改变他们生活的各种方式，他们做得很好，什么都搞定了。但实际上，这些东西中很少有真正那么好用、真正有效的。就像，别再假装你已经搞定一切了。

turns.en: I think it's much better to be humble about it and be like, wow, yeah, I don't know, this is changing quickly, and I'm just going to embrace it and see where it goes.
turns.zh: 我认为最好保持谦逊，就像，哇，是的，我不知道，这变化太快了，我只是要拥抱它，看看它会走向何方。

turns.en: Yeah, and that connects to what you said was a core component of people that are doing well right now: people that are curious and just kind of poking around and trying these things, and try them again because maybe it didn't work now. It didn't work before, now it works now.
turns.zh: 是的，这和你说的现在做得好的一个核心要素有关：那些好奇、到处摸索、尝试这些东西的人，他们会再试一次，因为也许现在没成功，以前没成功，但现在成功了。

turns.en: 100%. Yeah. It's like, every model, every new feature, it's like the people that are poking around at those edges, I've found, are just having such a blast doing it, you know.
turns.zh: 百分之百。是的。就像，每个模型、每个新功能，我发现那些在这些边缘摸索的人，他们做这件事的时候真的玩得很开心，你知道吗。

turns.en: And this connects to something else Kevin Weil, former CPO at OpenAI, said on the podcast, which has always stuck with me, which is the model we have today is the worst the model will ever be.
turns.zh: 这让我想起 OpenAI 前 CPO Kevin Weil 在播客上说过的一句话，我一直铭记在心，那就是我们今天拥有的模型是未来最差的模型。

turns.en: Exactly. I mean, that goes back to like when, you know, we, yeah. I mean, a new model comes out what, every week? I don't know, every day. Like, if you count all the labs and everything, it's changing so quickly and everyone gets better. And I don't know, it's like, I always try to remind myself, it must be like building or designing in the early days of computers, when componentry was evolving really quickly and there were these drastic step changes. You would hit these limitations and all of a sudden those limitations were gone. I think it's the same, right? These things just change, and what was totally broken yesterday now actually just kind of works.
turns.zh: 没错。我是说，这又回到了，你知道，我们，是的。我是说，新模型多久出一个？每周？我不知道，每天。如果你把所有实验室什么的都算上，变化太快了，而且都在变好。我不知道，就像，我总是提醒自己，这一定就像计算机早期时代的构建或设计，当时组件发展非常快，有这些剧烈的阶跃变化。你会遇到这些限制，然后突然这些限制就消失了。我想是一样的，对吧？这些东西就是会变，昨天还完全坏掉的东西，现在实际上就能用了。

turns.en: So maybe to start to close out the conversation, say a designer is listening to this and they're in that bucket of overwhelmed, anxious, struggling, stressed, feeling uncertain about their future.
turns.zh: 那么，也许在结束对话之前，假设有一位设计师正在听这个节目，他们正处于那种不知所措、焦虑、挣扎、压力重重、对未来感到不确定的状态。

turns.en: What's one suggestion you have for them to help them move out of that state and into a better place?
turns.zh: 你对他们有什么建议，帮助他们走出这种状态，进入更好的境地？

turns.en: Just recognizing that it's a totally rational feeling, and it's a great time to just try to explore and see what if I tried working, what if I tried rethinking the tooling, or what if I just embraced, like, oh, maybe I should prototype more. Let me try using these tools. But again, recognizing that—and maybe it helps to hear that—I think that we're all still so early, and it's still changing, and just kind of embracing that, like, just have fun with it and see where it goes. And I think maybe another thing I would say is really try to focus on the output, the outcome, right? At the end of the day, we're not here to build tools or processes. We're not here to build token max or something like that. We're here to make great software that people love, or great products, or whatever it is you do. But that's the thing that really matters. And if you focus on that, I think you'll hopefully find that these tools can help you do that, but you still have a huge role in that as the person that's kind of steering and directing it.
turns.zh: 只要认识到这是一种完全理性的感受，而且现在是尝试和探索的好时机——试试看如果我换个方式工作会怎样，如果我重新思考工具会怎样，或者如果我干脆接受“也许我该多做一些原型”会怎样。让我试试用这些工具。但再次强调，认识到——也许听到这个会有帮助——我觉得我们都还处于非常早期的阶段，一切仍在变化中，所以拥抱这一点，就像，玩得开心，看看它会走向何方。另外我想说的另一点是，真正专注于产出和结果，对吧？归根结底，我们不是来构建工具或流程的。我们不是来构建 token 最大化之类的东西。我们是来打造人们喜爱的优秀软件，或优秀产品，或无论你做什么。那才是真正重要的。如果你专注于这一点，我想你最终会发现这些工具能帮你做到，但作为掌舵和指引方向的人，你仍然扮演着巨大的角色。

transcript.sec: AI Corner: How AI Helps Ian

turns.en: So, along those lines, I'm going to take us to a couple recurring corners of the podcast. The first corner is AI corner. The question is just: what's one way that you have found AI to be really useful in your job that maybe might inspire someone to use, say, ChatGPT or Codex?
turns.zh: 沿着这个思路，我要带我们进入播客的几个固定环节。第一个环节是 AI 角落。问题是：你发现 AI 在你的工作中有哪些真正有用的方式，也许能激励别人去使用，比如 ChatGPT 或 Codex？

turns.en: As like a designer, I mean, nowadays I spend less time in the pixels. But I really do use it to kind of help me think through broader ideas. Or maybe, you know, I'll have an idea at night or something, and then I'll just like quickly type it in and have it like prototype something, and it'll give me like an idea that I can go and talk to the team about, and it helps visualize something. And so that's like a part of the design process. It's like early ideas or we're riffing through something, and I've found that ChatGPT, whether it's ChatGPT work or Codex, can really kind of help me visualize that. That's been something that's been really fun. And then there's more of the operation side, you know, it's like I have it now checking and making sure that important Slack messages that I need to follow up on are summarized and giving me context before important meetings, or for recruiting, or for every part of my process. I use this to kind of augment the work that I do.
turns.zh: 作为设计师，我的意思是，如今我在像素上花的时间少了。但我确实用它来帮助我思考更广泛的想法。或者，也许，你知道，我晚上会有一个想法，然后我就会快速输入，让它原型化一些东西，它会给我一个想法，我可以去和团队讨论，它帮助可视化某些东西。所以那是设计过程的一部分。就像早期想法，或者我们在即兴发挥某个东西，我发现 ChatGPT，无论是 ChatGPT 工作还是 Codex，都能真正帮助我将其可视化。那一直是非常有趣的事情。然后还有更多运营方面，你知道，我现在让它检查并确保我需要跟进的 Slack 重要消息被总结，并在重要会议前给我背景信息，或者用于招聘，或者用于我流程的每个部分。我用它来增强我所做的工作。

turns.en: It makes sense. On the prototyping piece, just to give someone a tip on how to do this. Are you opening up on your phone and firing off just like a Codex thread? What's like the mechanic of doing this?
turns.zh: 有道理。关于原型制作这部分，只是为了给别人一个如何做的提示。你是在手机上打开并启动一个 Codex 线程吗？这样做的机制是什么？

turns.en: ChatGPT work has been incredible because it now runs fully in the cloud, right? And so the idea is you can kind of just be anywhere and sort of talk to chat and have it really spend the time and come back with like a really great artifact. So I've found that it's been really fun to just be like, "Hey, you know, we're working on, I don't know, whatever this thing is, like whether it's helped me think through it or, you know, yeah, sometimes I will just have some ideas that I would love to see quickly visualized before I even take it further, and it will just kind of help me play with it and try it and stuff." And so that's been really fun. The fact that it's so accessible, right? Like I might not even be near a computer, or I can, you know, just kind of have that flexibility. I think is really fun.
turns.zh: ChatGPT 工作一直令人难以置信，因为它现在完全在云端运行，对吧？所以这个想法是，你可以随时随地，和聊天对话，让它真正花时间，然后带回一个非常棒的成果。所以我发现，只要说“嘿，你知道，我们在做，我不知道，不管是什么东西，无论是它帮助我思考，还是，你知道，是的，有时我只是有一些想法，我希望在进一步推进之前快速可视化，它就会帮助我摆弄它，尝试它之类的”，这真的很有趣。而且它如此易于访问，对吧？比如我可能甚至不在电脑旁，或者我可以，你知道，拥有那种灵活性。我觉得这真的很有趣。

turns.en: Awesome. Okay, I'm going to take us to another corner, fail corner.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，我要带我们进入另一个环节，失败角落。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: So the reason I do this is a lot of awesome people like yourself come on the podcast, and all people hear is all the amazing things they've done, all the ways they've been really successful, and they don't hear all the times things didn't work out. And I feel like that's very important for people to hear. It's not always up into the right and success. What's a story of a time you failed in your career, and what did you learn from that?
turns.zh: 我这样做是因为很多像你这样的优秀人士来到播客，人们听到的都是他们做过的所有了不起的事情，他们成功的所有方式，而他们听不到所有事情不顺利的时候。我觉得这对人们来说非常重要。并不总是一帆风顺和成功。你职业生涯中失败的一次经历是什么？你从中学到了什么？

tldr.zh: AI 已是出色的产品设计师，但理解用户需求、持有观点仍是人类优势。

tldr.en: Embrace adaptability and rapid iteration with AI tools; focus on outcomes, not traditional processes.
tldr.zh: 拥抱适应性和 AI 工具的快速迭代；关注结果而非传统流程。

qs.en: Why are designers currently the most unhappy in tech?
qs.zh: 为什么设计师目前是科技行业中最不开心的？

qs.en: How does AI change the role of designers?
qs.zh: AI 如何改变设计师的角色？

qs.en: What advice would you give to designers starting today?
qs.zh: 对于今天起步的设计师，你有什么建议？
